claim: For the simultaneous state-estimation/discrimination likelihood proposed by Ježek, joint optimization over the unknown density operators and the discrimination POVM is neither jointly concave nor jointly convex. On the feasible commuting-qubit slice \(\rho_1(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p,1-p)\), \(\rho_2=I/2\), \(\Pi_1(q)=\operatorname{diag}(q,1-q)\), and \(\Pi_2=I-\Pi_1\), choose a fixed computational-basis calibration measurement for \(\rho_1\) with frequencies \(1/2,1/2\). At \(p=q=1/2\), the Hessian of the source log-likelihood restricted to \((p,q)\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}-4&4\\4&0\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(-16\) and whose eigenvalues are \(-2\pm2\sqrt5\). Thus the source statement that convexity guarantees a unique global maximum or a plateau cannot serve as a global-optimality justification for the joint iteration. This result does not assert that the iteration must fail or that a particular data set has a spurious local maximum; it proves that a separate global convergence or optimality argument is required once states and measurement are optimized simultaneously.

integrity.computational_dependence: none for proof; exact-rational replay supplementary

scientific_limitations: The result disproves joint convexity/concavity and the associated universal uniqueness justification; it does not prove iteration failure on a particular data set.
The commuting-qubit slice does not classify all stationary points of the full matrix problem.
A differently phrased later optimization treatment may contain an equivalent source-specific observation.
title: Joint state–measurement likelihood in partial-information discrimination is not jointly concave
